items.title: Que sont-ils devenus ?Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé, du riff de guitare au tir de précision avec le « Super Lion »
items.description: Officier de gendarmerie à la retraite, le lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé est l’un de ces monstres sacrés à la double vie. Membre fondateur de l’éternel orchestre du « Super Lion » de la gendarmerie nationale de Guinée, ce virtuose a également prêté son talent à plusieurs autres formations mythiques du pays. ​Né en 1947 à Koumbia, dans la préfecture de Gaoual, le jeune Mamadou Bobo quitte tôt les bancs de l’école primaire pour suivre son instinct. Très vite, son chemin s'illumine sous une double étoile : celle des cuivres et des cordes d'un côté, celle des galons et du treillis de l'autre. ​Entre formations musicales légendaires et postes de responsabilité au sein de la maréchaussée, l'homme de Koumbia a mené une vie à cent à l'heure. Dans cet entretien à bâtons rompus, le vieux soldat repasse le film de son existence, oscillant avec la même aisance entre la flûte traversière, le saxo, la guitare solo et le fusil à l'épaule. ​Plongée dans un destin hors norme. Lisez ! ​ Guinéenews : Bonjour mon Lieutenant-colonel, dites-nous comment vous vous êtes retrouvé dans la musique ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : J’ai commencé la musique grâce à l'un de mes enseignants de l’école primaire nommé Mamy Kouyaté, originaire de Coyah. Il avait sa guitare et animait les bals poussière à l'époque coloniale à Koumbia. Prédisposé à la musique, je possédais une flûte anglaise à 9 trous dont je jouais tant bien que mal. Mon maître n’a découvert que tardivement mon talent pour la manipulation de cet instrument, et cela s’est passé au grand marché de Koumbia. Depuis lors, je suis devenu son second pour l’animation des bals poussière. C’est ainsi que j’ai commencé à pratiquer la musique. ​ Guinéenews : À l’époque, comment vous êtes-vous procuré cette flûte anglaise à 9 trous ? ​Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : J’ai acheté cette flûte directement à Koumbia. ​ Guinéenews : Peut-on connaître la suite de votre parcours ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : La suite de mon parcours s’est dessinée lorsque je suis arrivé à Labé. J’ai été recruté, comme plusieurs autres jeunes, au sein de l'orchestre de la ville. ​ Guinéenews : Vous faites allusion au Kolima Jazz de Labé ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Non ! Il s’agissait à l’époque de l’orchestre dénommé le « Léléna Jazz ». Il n'a changé de nom qu'après la construction du palais de la KOLIMA de Labé : le jour de l’inauguration, il a pris le nom de « Kolima Jazz ». Si j’ai bonne mémoire, ce jour-là, nous avions animé la ville de Labé pendant 5 jours en compagnie du Bembeya Jazz. ​ Guinéenews : Pouvez-vous nous citer les noms de quelques-uns de vos confrères de l’époque au sein de cet orchestre ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Voici la composition de l’orchestre dont je me souviens : le chef d’orchestre Sampil (trompette), Dieng (saxo alto), Lansana Condé de Dabola (guitare solo), Diély Sory (guitare médium), Diéli Kèmo (saxo ténor), moi-même (saxo ténor), Souleymane Sylla (clarinette et saxo), Sény (tumbiste), ainsi que d’autres musiciens dont je n’ai plus les noms en tête. ​ Guinéenews : Après le « Léléna Jazz » devenu le « Kolima Jazz », parlez-nous de la suite de votre carrière. ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Je suis rentré chez moi à Gaoual, où j’ai appartenu pendant un court moment à l’orchestre local, dirigé à l’époque par feu Elhadj Binani Diallo, qui était alors directeur d’école. ​Le destin étant inéluctable, c’est à Gaoual, en passant devant une école, que j’ai vu une foule attroupée pour un concours de recrutement au compte de l’usine textile de Sanoyah. Sans hésiter, je me suis présenté et j'ai été admis comme employé de cette usine. ​ Guinéenews : Votre parcours de musicien s’est-il arrêté là au sein de l’usine textile de Sanoyah ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Non ! J’ai travaillé pendant quelques mois dans cette usine. Par mesure de sécurité au travail, les Anglais nous dotaient de pommades pour protéger nos yeux contre les infections dues au traitement du coton. Au bout de deux semaines, les stocks étant épuisés et sans aucune protection pour nos yeux, j’ai décidé de démissionner. J’ai préféré préserver ma vue plutôt que de privilégier l’argent. Remarquez bien, c’est depuis cette époque que j’ai les yeux rouges ! ​ Guinéenews : Avez-vous connu d’autres péripéties au cours de votre parcours musical ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : J’ai joué un temps dans l’orchestre du 5ᵉ arrondissement, puis j'ai poursuivi au camp Alpha Yaya dans le même registre. Lors d’une soirée avec l’orchestre du camp, au vu de mes prestations au saxo, le capitaine Ousmane Condé, alors commandant du camp, a été informé de ma présence. ​Dans cet orchestre, Babady était le chef. Immédiatement, on m’a fait revêtir l’uniforme de soldat. On m’a ensuite contraint à jouer de la guitare basse, tenue jusqu'alors par le caporal Morlaye, qui avait ses limites. J’ai écopé de plusieurs billets d’écrou de sa part lorsque j’ai commencé à être apprécié à ce poste (rires). Il a fallu l’intervention du sergent-chef Babady pour que je retrouve la tranquillité. ​ Guinéenews : Comment êtes-vous devenu par la suite guitariste accompagnateur ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : C’est grâce à Jean Keita, qui faisait également partie de l’orchestre du camp Alpha Yaya, que j’ai finalement maîtrisé la guitare (médium et accompagnement). ​Il m’avait pris sous son aile chez lui, près de l’hôtel Gbessia, alors qu’il était nouvellement marié. Il m’a encouragé à m'exercer seul au départ, puis il a décelé mes aptitudes. Au bout de 2 ans, j’ai appris sa rapidité, son sens de la mélodie et surtout sa rigueur face à l’instrument. ​L’actuel Général Bassamba continue de m’appeler « Guantanaméra ». C’est le sobriquet que j’avais reçu au sein de l’orchestre du camp Alpha Yaya, car j’étais l’un des premiers à interpréter ce morceau légendaire. Beaucoup ne connaissaient pas mon vrai nom au camp : pour me trouver, il fallait demander « GUANTANAMERA ». ​Plus tard, frustré par le comportement de certains hauts officiers de l’armée d’alors — dont je tairai les noms et pour lesquels je prie le ciel —, j’ai déserté et quitté cet orchestre. ​ Guinéenews : Après avoir quitté l’armée, de quoi vous êtes-vous occupé ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Bald é : J’ai été sollicité à ma grande surprise par les autorités de Forécariah, qui recherchaient des musiciens. Le choix s’est porté sur moi et j’ai fini par accepter, non sans difficulté. Il a fallu qu'ils me fournissent des vêtements et une valise remplie à partir du marché de Madina avant que je ne m’embarque dans cette aventure. J’ai passé plus d’un an au sein de l’orchestre de Forécariah. ​Un jour, lors d’une visite à Conakry pour voir ma famille, je suis repassé voir mon maître Jean Keita au camp Alpha Yaya en pleine soirée. Il m’a cédé la guitare et, après ma prestation, le capitaine Ansou Condé, commandant de la garde républicaine du camp Boiro, m’a tendu une autre perche. ​Arrivé au camp Boiro, il m'a proposé d’intégrer l’orchestre de la garde républicaine. C’est ainsi que j’ai renfilé la tenue, cette fois avec le grade de brigadier. J’ai donc évolué au sein de cet ensemble orchestral, tandis que le maître Kèlètigui me sollicitait de temps à autre pour jouer à ses côtés. ​ Guinéenews : En tant que membre fondateur du Super Lion de la Gendarmerie nationale, comment avez-vous intégré cette formation ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Au début, je m’occupais également de l’encadrement des musiciennes de l’orchestre Les Amazones de Guinée. C’est à cette période que j’ai eu l’idée de proposer à l’état-major la création d’un orchestre masculin pour le compte de la gendarmerie nationale. ​J’ai été chargé du recrutement des musiciens de la formation, qui a plus tard été baptisée le « SUPER LION » de la gendarmerie nationale. Pour le recrutement des éléments, j’avais des convocations vierges signées par le chef d’état-major. Je suis donc membre fondateur de cet orchestre et c’est moi qui ai recruté l'ensemble des membres de cette première mouture. Guineenews : Pouvez-vous nous donner la composition par section du tout premier ensemble du Super Lion ? ​ Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Pour la section guitare : Mamadou Bobo Baldé (guitare accompagnement), Soumah Ismael « S » (guitare basse), Sékouba Diabaté (guitare solo). À la section cuivres : Mamadou Diallo (saxo alto), Charles Soumah (trompette). Enfin : Khaly (batterie), Wright Edouard (chant) et Philippe Gérard (chant). Guinéenews : Plusieurs orchestres ont été créés au sein de l’armée guinéenne. Quelle place occupait le Super Lion par rapport aux autres ? ​Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Le Super Lion de la gendarmerie nationale était un orchestre de premier plan. Après seulement un mois de répétitions, l’ensemble était déjà opérationnel, et c'est à ce moment-là que nous avons été invités au Sénégal pour des prestations. Nous avons brillé sur tous les podiums de la capitale et de l’intérieur du pays avec des compositions musicales de haute facture. ​ Guinéenews : En quelle année avez-vous quitté l’orchestre du Super Lion ? ​Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : J’ai quitté l’orchestre après l’agression portugaise du 22 novembre 1970. Cela s'est fait à la suite d’une permission accordée pour aller chevet de ma mère malade : à mon retour, j’ai trouvé qu'on m'avait remplacé par François Touré et j'ai été directement nommé chef de poste au Palais du Peuple. J’y ai vu une porte de sortie favorable, car mes parents n’ont jamais voulu que je joue de la guitare. ​ Guinéenews : Vous avez été fonctionnaire, quels sont les postes que vous avez occupés au cours de votre carrière ? ​Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : J’ai occupé plusieurs postes au sein de la gendarmerie nationale. À Kindia, où j'ai passé 13 ans, j’ai été cumulativement secrétaire, agent de constat, agent de recherche, chargé de la billetterie, chargé du ravitaillement et délégué syndical. ​J’ai aussi servi à Madina Oula, puis comme commandant de brigade à Kankalabé, Dalaba centre, Gaoual, Kassa, Beyla, Tougué, Fria… ​J’ai également travaillé comme officier central à la RTG, à la Banque centrale, à la BICIGUI… J’ai finalement pris ma retraite en 2011 à la gendarmerie de Dixinn. ​ Guinéenews : Qu’est-ce que la musique vous a apporté tout au long de votre parcours ? ​Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Je suis fier d’avoir servi la musique guinéenne et d’avoir apporté ma contribution à son développement. Sur le plan humain, j’ai tissé d'excellentes relations qui durent encore aujourd'hui. J’ai acquis une certaine notoriété et je ne regrette absolument pas d’avoir servi mon pays. ​ Guinée news : Bénéficiez-vous de droits d’auteur de la part du BGDA (Bureau Guinéen du Droit d'Auteur) et d'une prise en charge sanitaire ? ​Lieuten ant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : Je ne bénéficie ni de droits d’auteur ni de prise en charge sanitaire. ​J’avoue que c’est certainement de ma faute, car je ne m’y suis pas intéressé en raison de mon éloignement de la capitale. Je vis aujourd'hui à Gaoual, et je serais très heureux de trouver des personnes prêtes à m’aider à faire valoir mes droits. ​ Guinéenews : Pour clore cet entretien, quel message aimeriez-vous adresser aux jeunes musiciens guinéens ? ​Lieutenant-colonel Mamadou Bobo Baldé : J’encourage la jeunesse à persévérer et à puiser dans les racines de la musique guinéenne. Je souhaite qu’ils véhiculent dans leurs chansons des messages de paix et de bonheur. Les jeunes musiciens doivent prendre exemple sur leurs devanciers qui ont su valoriser la musique guinéenne à tous les niveaux. Bon courage à tous ! ​ Entretien réalisé par LY Abdoul pour Guinéenews.

items.title: 1 killed, 3 wounded as Iranian commercial ship hit in Hormuz Strait
items.description: At least one person was killed, and three others were wounded after an Iranian commercial ship was targeted by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday morning, the country's state-run IRIB news agency reported. The vessel was struck off the coasts of Iran's southern Hengam and Qeshm islands at 5:00 a.m. local time (0130 GMT), the IRIB said, citing Qeshm County Governor Hossein Amir Teymouri. The type of projectile was not yet known, he added. The Strait of Hormuz has witnessed repeated attacks on commercial ships and warships since early this year. Following US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, Tehran restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, US forces imposed a naval blockade targeting vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports and coastal areas. The US Central Command said on Wednesday that its forces had "destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers" in response to Iran's targeting of "a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days." Iran responded by targeting two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Gulf and firing missiles at a US air base in Jordan. (Cover: Numerous merchant ships belonging to Iran and other countries remain at anchor in the Strait of Hormuz in Bandar Abbas, Iran, September 10, 2026. /VCG)

items.title: Sécurité de Kaliningrad : Moscou prend «toutes les mesures nécessaires» face aux manœuvres de l’OTAN
items.description: La Russie prend « toutes les mesures necessaires » pour assurer la securite de la region de Kaliningrad, a declare a Izvestia le porte-parole du Kremlin, Dmitri Peskov. Il a egalement estime que l'intensification de l'activite militaire de l'OTAN a proximite de cette region etait evidente aux yeux de Moscou. Ces declarations interviennent apres les propos tenus le 11 septembre par le ministre polonais des Affaires etrangeres, Radoslaw Sikorski, qui a appele l'OTAN a multiplier les exercices militaires aux abords de Kaliningrad. Le chef de la diplomatie polonaise a toutefois ecarte toute possibilite d'une prise de controle de l'enclave russe. La Russie a exprime a plusieurs reprises son inquietude face a l'activite sans precedent de l'OTAN a ses frontieres occidentales. Fin juillet 2025, Nikolaï Patrouchev, conseiller du president russe, avait ainsi souligne que la region de la mer Baltique, autrefois paisible, se transformait, « sous l'effet des efforts des pays de l'OTAN », en une zone de « tensions et d'instabilite militaro-politique ». Le Kremlin affirme de son cote que la Russie ne menace aucun pays, tout en assurant qu'elle repondra a toute initiative qu'elle jugerait susceptible de porter atteinte a ses interets ou a sa securite. L'hysterie de l'Occident face a la pretendue « menace russe » dure depuis plusieurs annees deja, mais le president Vladimir Poutine a explique a maintes reprises que la Russie n'avait pas l'intention d'attaquer les pays de l'OTAN, car cela n'avait aucun sens. Les responsables politiques occidentaux continuent neanmoins d'effrayer regulierement leurs populations en entretenant la perception d'une « menace russe » afin de justifier le renforcement militaire de l'Alliance et de detourner l'attention de difficultes interieures.

items.title: Tunisie | Me Ghazi Mrabet et six co-accusés déférés devant le juge d’instruction
items.description: L’avocat Ghazi Mrabet et six autres suspects — dont un trafiquant de drogue connu des services — seront déférés devant le juge d’instruction du Pôle judiciaire économique et financier de Tunis, leur garde à vue ayant été prolongée dans le cadre de l’enquête. Cette mesure, décidée, avant-hier, vendredi 11 septembre 2026, s’inscrit dans le cadre des investigations en cours concernant une suspicion de détention de stupéfiants. L’affaire a débuté lorsque l’avocat a été surpris au domicile du deuxième suspect — un trafiquant de drogue faisant l’objet d’une condamnation par contumace à 40 ans de prison, qui serait l’un de ses clients, selon plusieurs de ses collègues. Lors de l’opération, les autorités ont saisi 8 kg de cocaïne, 40 plaquettes de résine de cannabis ( zatla ) et une somme d’argent estimée à 394 000 dinars. À la suite de l’ouverture de l’enquête, quatre autres suspects ont été arrêtés, tandis qu’un célèbre footballeur, dont le nom n’a pas été divulgué, a été déféré devant le parquet. La semaine dernière, le ministère public près le Tribunal de première instance de Tunis a ordonné aux agents de la sous-direction de lutte contre les stupéfiants (relevant de la direction de la police judiciaire) de placer en garde à vue l’avocat Ghazi Mrabet ainsi que le trafiquant de drogue en question. Leur garde à vue a été fixée à cinq jours pour des chefs d’accusation incluant la constitution d’un réseau de trafic de drogue et le blanchiment d’argent. Les deux hommes ont été interpellés au domicile du trafiquant recherché ; la perquisition des lieux a permis la saisie d’importantes quantités de stupéfiants. Selon l’agence Tap, citant une source judiciaire, Me Mrabet, qui se trouvait en compagnie du trafiquant de drogue, a tenté d’entraver le travail des agents de la police judiciaire pour permettre la fuite de son client, mais ces derniers sont parvenus à les interpeller tous deux. I. B. L’article Tunisie | Me Ghazi Mrabet et six co-accusés déférés devant le juge d’instruction est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Kremlin not ruling out return to Ukraine talks in October
items.description: Three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the United States on ending Europe’s worst conflict since World War II could take place in October, the Kremlin said on Sunday, according to Russian media. “We do not rule out such a possibility; we are talking about the foreseeable future,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists, cited by Russia’s Ria and Tass news agencies. For all the latest headlines, follow our Google News channel online or via the app. Washington is seeking to kick-start long-stalled efforts hoping to put an end to the more than four-year-long war, with US negotiators visiting Kyiv and Moscow and US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin holding talks over the phone. Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed, while US-led efforts stalled with Trump’s attention diverted to the ongoing US-Israeli war in the Middle East with Iran. In an interview released on Saturday, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December for talks. But Peskov immediately ruled it out as “impossible,” speaking to AFP in New Delhi on Saturday, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting could only take place in the Russian capital. Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for a face-to-face sit-down with Zelenskyy aimed at brokering an end to the conflict, which has killed thousands of people and crippled both countries’ economies. Both Moscow and Kyiv have escalated long-range strikes on each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war. Previous rounds of talks have foundered, with Moscow so far unwilling to drop its maximalist conditions to end the fighting, including a demand that Ukraine cede territory in the east that Russia’s troops have not captured. On Sunday, Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov told journalists, including from AFP, that there is so far no “coordinated package” on which negotiations could be based. “At present, there is the idea that we need to reach an agreement on the territorial issue. But there are also many other questions,” he added. Read more: Kyiv preparing for talks to resume in October, senior Ukrainian official says

items.title: This Is What Women’s Self-Defense Looks Like
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. O n the first day of self-defense class, I learn to say “no.” We’re in a Southern California martial-arts studio not far from an In-N-Out Burger. The space smells faintly of cooked meat. I’m one of six students, all women: four nurses, one flight attendant, and me. In this introductory session, we’re supposed to get a taste of what it means to protect ourselves—and, if necessary, to fight back. For the longest time, I had wondered what it would be like to hit someone. Like, really hit them. I had grown up understanding that women aren’t supposed to engage in fantasies about violence, which is to say that we aren’t really supposed to think about it. But many of us do. All the time. Violence can, of course, affect anyone. It is in our homes and neighborhoods and in the news; it is experienced person to person, nation to nation, directly and indirectly. But for women especially, even when violence is not an immediate physical reality, what is real is the constant threat of it . In my experience, this sense of threat doesn’t change as time goes on. So in late 2023, I signed up for self-defense classes with a training program called Impact Personal Safety. I was working on a book exploring the ways in which women and girls are socialized not to say “no,” even to people who threaten them. But I also just wanted to understand what it is for “no” to be expressed in the body—what it means to feel the “no.” Our lead instructor, Dawn Hofmeister, is in her 50s and petite. She stands straight and appears to glide through the air, and although I’m much larger than she is, I feel submissive in her presence. She teaches alongside a couple of female assistants and a male sparring partner, Matt Harris. A middle-aged man with doe-like eyes, Harris tells the assembled group that he will be playing the role of our assailant that day, a character named Billy. Everyone likes Harris. Nobody likes Billy. Billy emerges after Harris slips on a padded suit and helmet. In the scenarios we’re thrown into, Billy is aggressive. He walks right at us, his voice raised. He can also be sneaky: Sometimes, he’ll sidle up in a bumbling, faux-friendly way before lunging. Other times, he appears to be severely mentally ill, or under the influence of drugs, or perfectly sober but intensely pushy. He asks for things (the time, a cellphone) or whether we need something—help with our groceries? A ride? When we rebuff him, he starts toward us with purpose. “No!” we yell. This is supposed to come after some effort at placating him— I don’t need a ride, thank you ; I think the person you’re looking for went the other way —a tactic that, in these scenarios, does not work, in that it does not thwart Billy from approaching, bull-like, with apparent malicious intent. Hofmeister explains that she teaches students to say “no” repeatedly and often because it helps strengthen a woman’s resolve to assert her boundaries and puts a potential assailant on notice that what he’s about to do is undesired. She adds that the word can increase the power of a physical blow and disrupt a freeze response, keeping the woman breathing through her counterattack. Along with saying “no,” we’re taught the palm-heel strike—heels of the hands up and together, palms facing outward, ready to hit—the first line of physical defense in a sequence of moves and postures meant to end with Billy on his back or side, writhing. The second move is a strong knee to the groin. The third, once he’s down, is a knee or stomp to the head. Billy takes a fair amount of abuse. Sometimes I worry about Harris, the human being inside the padded suit, especially when he is slow to get back on his feet. But feeling bad for Billy, I realize, is part of what I’m trying to undo: the internalized empathy response that can make people, especially women, afraid to hit another person, or lead them to give bad actors the benefit of the doubt even while the voice in their own head is saying danger . When Billy advances toward us, my first “no” is the weakest. But then my hands go up and I yell “No!” with more force. Billy falls, and I jab my heel into his chin. My knee goes to his groin—another “No!” Soon the no ’s are coming quickly and easily, and by the time Billy is splayed on the ground, I’m hovering over him—like Muhammad Ali standing over Sonny Liston in that famous 1965 photo—and practically screaming. C ontemporary self-defense courses recognize that protecting oneself involves a lot more than elbowing an assailant in the neck. As Susan Brownmiller put it in her 1975 book, Against Our Will: Men, Women and Rape , telling women to kick a man in the groin or stick a thumb in his eye is not enough—because first, women must overcome an aversion to hitting. Describing her time learning self-defense, she wrote that this inhibition “was so strong in each of us that on the first try none of us could make physical contact.” What women need, she argued, “is systemic training in self-defense that begins in childhood, so that the inhibition resulting from the prohibition may be overcome.” What many people think of as women’s self-defense tends to go by the designation Empowerment Self-Defense, or ESD. Also known as “feminist self-defense” and “holistic self-defense,” ESD posits that teaching nonphysical strategies is as important as teaching physical ones—because if a woman can recognize and thwart an attacker’s verbal intrusions early in an encounter, she is less likely to need to get physical. Impact Personal Safety, Southern California, the program I trained under, says that it has taught assertiveness, boundary-setting, deflection, and de-escalation to tens of thousands of students—plus the skills necessary for what the organization’s late founder, Lisa Gaeta, described as “causing a scene.” (Essentially: raising your voice and shouting things such as “Get away from me” and “I don’t want this,” which is harder to do than you might think.) That makes ESD different from mainstream self-defense, which “tends to be stranger-focused, sometimes fear-based, rather than empowerment-based,” Jocelyn Hollander, a University of Oregon sociology professor and self-defense instructor, told me. ESD’s emphasis on “internal” skills—emotional, psychological—is aimed at subverting behaviors that students might have adopted based on their gender or personal history, or in response to political and cultural messaging. Basically, Hollander said, the method gives women the tools they need to say no “to whatever someone wants to do to or with you.” ESD is applicable not only in extreme interactions but also in what some might call the more routine situations that many women experience, such as being coerced into sex. In Hollander’s classes, she has students turn to each other with a simple question—“Can I borrow your pencil?” or “Do you want to go have coffee?”—to which the other person then has to respond “No.” Usually, there’s a lot of nervous laughter, Hollander told me. Many students realize that they never say “no” to anybody. Or, when they do, they qualify it, soften it, make excuses. But once they discover that the world won’t end when they say “no,” Hollander observed, it can be a “huge epiphany.” Such training, Hollander’s research suggests, pays tangible dividends. Women who take ESD classes are less likely to be the victim of rape or sexual assault than women who do not. In a 2020 study of female college students involving nearly 300 women, Hollander found that those who had taken an ESD class had about 50 percent lower odds, on average, of experiencing any sort of assault over the one-year period following the course than those who had not taken a class. “I just have to point out that 50 percent is a huge decrease for an intervention,” she said. “Psychologists are usually happy if they get a few percentage points’ difference. Fifty percent is immense.” Her research has also found that many students experience increased “self-efficacy”—a sense that they can be effective in the world. And other research has found that this sort of self-defense training can reduce feelings of anxiety, depression, fear, and self-blame. Hollander’s results have been echoed in the work of other academics, including Charlene Senn, a University of Windsor psychology professor whose research focuses on male violence against women. Senn was inspired by the academics Patricia Rozee and Mary Koss, who in 2001 published a paper titled “ Rape: A Century of Resistance ,” which synthesized decades of research on sexual violence. They translated their analysis into a series of recommendations, such as giving women cognitive and emotional education to defend themselves against assault. Senn took those recommendations and set out to make them come alive. First, she created a program for university women called Enhanced Assess, Acknowledge, Act—a 12-hour, evidence-based training that, among other things, teaches women how to recognize a risk of sexual assault and then resist it. Then, from 2011 to 2013, she and a group of academics conducted a study of 893 female college freshmen in Canada, to test the program’s efficacy. Of the students, 451 were assigned to a “resistance group” and took EAAA classes, and 442 were put in a control group, which meant that they basically “went to a room,” Senn said, and read sexual-assault-prevention pamphlets distributed by their schools. [ Read: A recipe for sexual assault ] After the EAAA courses, Senn said, the resistance and control groups were given follow-up surveys at intervals of one week, six months, 12 months, and 18 months. The researchers found that one year after the EAAA training, the women in the resistance group were 46.3 percent less likely to have been raped and 63.2 percent less likely to have experienced attempted rape than the women in the control group. A later study by Senn and her colleagues, which looked at a broader, more diverse cohort of university women who took EAAA classes from 2017 to 2021, had similar findings: a 57.3 percent reduction in reports of rape and a 32.9 percent reduction in attempted rape six months after the training. To me, these results were nothing short of stunning. I wondered why data like these hadn’t been publicized more widely. Jill Cermele, a psychology professor at Drew University, told me that this was partly because of ideology. Cermele co-authored a 2022 paper with Martha McCaughey, an academic specializing in women’s studies and the author of Real Knockouts: The Physical Feminism of Women’s Self-Defense , about the ways in which the efficacy of self-defense has been neglected or ignored by both public-health officials and anti-rape activists—some of whom contend that emphasizing the need for women to learn self-defense serves only to put the onus on them, rather than on men. Cermele said she believes that this logic is misguided—that no matter people’s views on blame, anyone who cares about women’s safety has “a professional and a moral obligation to pay attention to the data.” That said, “one of the things that psychology tells us is that people are not convinced by data—they’re convinced by stories.” D uring my next set of self-defense classes, things take a darker turn. The 16-hour “basics” training unfolds over the course of two weekends, with a new cohort of students. Our lead instructor is Dani, a young woman who took her first Impact class when she was only 6. Our padded assailant is Michael Peñafiel, a middle-aged father of a young son. Like Harris, our attacker from the intro class, Peñafiel has an alter ego: Kane. On Day 1, we hit, we kick, we send knees into Kane’s groin. Yet the stakes feel somehow lower. Partly, it’s the absurdity of Kane’s outfit—a suit of hard plastic, foam, and duct tape, with a harness-like thing slung between his legs and around his waist. His helmet makes him look like a bug. The padding forces hims to move around the studio with his hips thrust forward. But then comes Day 2: what we glibly call “sexual-assault day.” Our instructors teach us how to fend off an assailant who approaches while we’re lying on our side, and demands that we get into positions that could—quickly, disturbingly, unmistakably—leave us open to assault. We get down on hands and knees. We lie flat on our backs. Today, our attacker is closer, the interaction more intimate. This makes everything scarier and can provoke a freeze response that feels impossible to overcome. [ Read: Everything we know about rape is wrong ] Kane gets behind me, clutches my arms, and pins me to the floor. He crouches on his knees, breathing heavily over me. I think: Maybe if I just lie here, he will go away . I’m surprised at how heavy he is and how difficult it is to imagine freeing myself from his grasp. He hisses instructions. “What’s going on?” I ask him. We’re supposed to say this phrase out loud, not so much to prompt a reasonable answer but to remind ourselves that we are being attacked in the first place. He merely mumbles. Dani tells me to roll onto my back, which is the last thing I want to do. “Be patient,” she says. “He’s going to make a mistake.” And make a mistake he does. As Kane tries to position himself directly on top of me, he releases one of my arms and up it goes, my fingers in a beak-like shape, directed at his eyes. “Eyes! Eyes! Eyes!” everyone yells. I stab at the netting on his padded helmet, and Kane falls backward. Then I get into a kick position, leg in the air and ready to strike—his head, his torso, his groin, wherever I can find a target. After a few kicks, Kane finally goes down, at which point I pull myself up and run around to the top of his head to assess that he’s indeed knocked out. Finally, I run away, keeping in mind the final step: go get help. I should acknowledge that self-defense techniques may not help in situations when it is impossible or dangerous for a woman to fight back—such as when she is incapacitated, or when an assailant is armed and threatening deadly force. And it is fair to argue that the potential perpetrators of violence, not their victims, should be the ones subject to intervention and training. But Impact’s founder, Gaeta, who died last year, had no patience for the argument that to avoid victim blaming, women should not be taught to defend themselves. People say, “Well, we should make men be better,” she once told me. “How the fuck am I going to make men be better?” [ Read: Not all men, but any man ] The point about responsibility is not a new argument. In the ’80s and ’90s, for instance, some feminist activists began to express concern that teaching women self-defense was akin to engaging in victim blaming —so the practice became “unfashionable in a way,” Hollander told me. She added that yes, ideally, more men would move through life with the explicit understanding that they should not assault women, “but from a researcher’s perspective, we have no clue how to make that happen.” No intervention has been shown to meaningfully reduce perpetration. “And what are we supposed to do in the meantime?” Hollander said. “Just sit around and wait for the revolution?” Some researchers argue that when it comes to men, self-defense training for women can move the needle in an important way—by shifting men’s own understanding of their place in the world. “Changing men does not necessarily entail intervening directly with men,” Hollander wrote in a 2018 article. Quoting a paper by the masculinity researcher Michael Flood, she added, “Empowering women may transform gender relations by ‘shifting the wider conditions within which men make choices about violence and non-violence.’” T he third day of basics class is the day I start crying. We’re learning how to react defensively and offensively: Many of the techniques involve moving toward our assailant, not away from him. This is counterintuitive—instinctively, one wants to retreat from danger—but being able to inflict real damage and disable an attacker means having to get up close. The disabling doesn’t go well for me. About three hours into the class, I’m thrown to the mat and pinned. Kane is on top of me and feels stronger and heavier than usual, more hell-bent on restraining me. Just when I think I’ve started to get away, he grabs me again and pins me on my side, my back to him, my arms folded in front of me. I freeze. The instructors and other students yell words of encouragement—“He’s going to make a mistake!” someone calls—but I can’t move. The words are meaningless. Adrenalin is making me tremble. After what seems like an eternity, Kane seems to ease up a bit, and I’m able to turn toward him, hit him, and stumble away. I make my way to Gaeta—present that day, watching from a table at one end of the studio—who asks, “What happened?” The question is part of the drill. After the fight, we’re supposed to describe in as much detail as possible what occurred and what our attacker looked like, to practice how, in the real world, we might give specific information about an assault to a friend or law-enforcement officer. I’m not sure what to tell her, but I try: “He attacked me. He threw me to the ground. I tried to get up and almost succeeded, but he pinned me back down.” I feel shame and embarrassment rising, and I begin to cry. I run to the line of students assembled against a wall. One says, “Good job.” The others don’t know what to say. Neither do I. I just stand there with tears streaming, my heart thumping. Two weeks after my graduation from the class, I’m stuck on that memory, of an encounter that felt like failure. Peñafiel has since clarified that he did not, in fact, ease up on me. He also said that my reaction—freezing, crying—is not uncommon. Driving home from that class, shaken, I had called my friend Nancy, a documentary filmmaker whose work has focused largely on sexual assault. She tried to put what had happened to me into perspective: I got scared, she said, and felt shame and embarrassment, which came not only from being scared but also from my sense that I hadn’t fought back in the “right” way. About a week after the class, I also spoke with one of Impact’s assistant instructors, Amanda Hall, who is also a reality-TV producer. She told me that she has seen this sort of response many times. She herself cried during the opening drill in her first class. The adrenaline can be “really activating,” she said. “It’s scary no matter what.” I try to give myself a little grace. After all, I was able to finish the fight. This reminds me of something that Cermele, the psychology professor, told me: Many people mistakenly believe that once an assault happens or starts, you have to somehow wait until the assailant is finished. This is not always the case. “Unfortunately, assaults take time,” she said, which means “multiple opportunities for resistance. And if I couldn’t organize myself to resist in the beginning, if I was too drunk, if I was too afraid, if I was whatever, there might still be a moment where I can do something with that. And I think we miss that by not talking about resistance. It’s very all-or-nothing.” She told me about a student who, after learning self-defense techniques one semester, was assaulted by a male friend’s roommate at a college party. During the attack, the woman was able to summon her skills and fight him off. “We would call that a success story,” Cermele said. “The assault ended because of what she did, not because he decided it was over.” I now know what it feels like to hit someone. I also can’t stop thinking about how different the world might be if more girls and women were taught to defend themselves. We might see the number of assaults against women cut in half. We might see more teenagers like a self-defense student who told me that now she knows how to use her voice: “I feel like I’m a powerful person.” We would see more women learning to shout “No!” and enjoying, with much less fear, what one instructor called “a bigger life”—the kind of life every one of us deserves. ​​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Mali : une première opération réussie pour séparer des bébés siamois
items.description: Une equipe medicale pluridisciplinaire malienne a realise avec succes une intervention chirurgicale visant a separer deux nourrissons siamois au Centre hospitalier universitaire (CHU) Gabriel-Toure de Bamako. L'operation, realisee 9 septembre, constitue une premiere dans le pays. Les deux fillettes sont nees le 29 août par cesarienne, au terme d'une grossesse au cours de laquelle des malformations congenitales avaient ete diagnostiquees. Elles etaient reliees par leurs systemes urinaire et digestif et partageaient notamment une meme vessie et un meme colon. Face a cette situation rare, le directeur general du CHU Gabriel-Toure, le professeur Thierno Madani Diop, a mobilise une equipe composee notamment de chirurgiens pediatriques, d'anesthesistes-reanimateurs, de cardiologues, de radiologues, de pharmaciens, de laborantins et de personnels paramedicaux du bloc operatoire. Apres plusieurs examens et diagnostics preoperatoires, les specialistes ont procede a l'intervention, dont le succes a ete salue par la ministre de la Sante et du Developpement social, Assa Badiallo Toure. Lors d'une visite au CHU, la ministre a qualifie l'intervention de « prouesse » et salue le travail des praticiens maliens. Selon les estimations citees par le ministere, les naissances de bebes siamois surviennent dans environ un cas sur 200 000 naissances. Cette reussite constitue une etape importante pour la medecine specialisee dans le pays et illustre les capacites des equipes medicales maliennes a prendre en charge des interventions chirurgicales complexes. Les jumeaux siamois apparaissent lorsqu'un embryon unique ne se separe pas completement au debut de la grossesse. La possibilite de les separer depend notamment des organes qu'ils partagent.

items.title: Boulkiemdé/Kindi : La mairie vole au secours des personnes vulnérables
items.description: BURKINA-BOULKIEMDE-KINDI-PERDONNES-VULNERABLES-SOUTIEN Boulkiemdé/Kindi : La mairie vole au secours des personnes vulnérables Kindi, 13 sept. 2026 (AIB) – La mairie de la commune rurale de Kindi a procédé le vendredi 11 septembre, à la remise de vivres au profit des personnes vulnérables de la localité, a constaté l'AIB. Composé de 44 sacs de maïs, de 21 sacs de riz de 25 kg et de 22 bidons d'huile de 5 litres, ce don est destiné aux veuves, aux personnes vivant avec un handicap ainsi qu'aux personnes déplacées internes (PDI). La cérémonie de remise a été présidée par le 2e vice-président, Bassolé, représentant le président de la délégation spéciale de Kindi, assisté du responsable du service social de la commune, Hamidou Kaboré. L’autorité communale a salué la résilience des bénéficiaires du jour tout en réitérant le soutien indéfectible de la municipalité à leur endroit. Elle a également salué le travail et le dévouement du service social aux côtés des couches vulnérables. Au nom des bénéficiaires, le responsable des personnes vivant avec un handicap, Barthélémy Zongo, a exprimé sa profonde gratitude à la mairie. Il a qualifié ce geste d'inestimable en cette période de soudure, tout en exhortant les autorités administratives à pérenniser et à multiplier de telles actions de solidarité à ces populations ne disposant pratiquement pas d'autres sources de soutien. Agence d'information du Burkina CS/PB/AS/ATA

Cette cérémonie a commencé par la montée des couleurs accompagnée de l'exécution du Ditanyè. Le PDS, Rateba Dawega, a, après son mot de bienvenue, appelé à la citoyenneté, à l'amour de la patrie et au soutien des FDS et VDP. Pour lui, la police a toujours été un vent favorable pour le bon déroulement des activités de la mairie et dans la collaboration avec la population. D'où sa reconnaissance à ce corps paramilitaire qui n'a eu de cesse dans l'exercice salutaire, de la tâche à elle confiée. Pour le Commissaire, Hubert Koama, c'est vraiment un honneur de partager ces moments avec la population. Il a réaffirmé son engagement et sa disponibilité pour le bien de la Commune. Il a remercié les autorités pour cet honneur et félicité les appelés à l'immersion patriotique pour leur preuve de patriotisme dans les activités depuis leur Sortie. Les différents chefs de services (santé animale, environnement, inspection primaire, lycée départemental, CVD ) ont tour à tour, témoigné leur reconnaissance sur la bonne collaboration avec la police et souhaité une bonne suite de carrière à tous. La cérémonie s'est conclue par des remerciements et des acclamations, signe de reconnaissance à la Police et aux VDP pour leur travail d'honneur abattue. Agence d'information du Burkina

items.title: Boulkiemdé/Poa : plus de 200 plants mis en terre lors d’une journée de reboisement
items.description: BURKINA-BOULKIEMDE-POA-REBOISEMENT Boulkiemdé/Poa : plus de 200 plants mis en terre lors d’une journée de reboisement Poa, 13 sept. 2026 (AIB) – Plus de 200 plants ont été mis en terre, samedi, à Poa, à l’occasion d’une journée de reboisement organisée par le promoteur de Lévis Agro-Sylvio-Pastoral, Lévi Zoubga. Cette première édition a réuni des jeunes, des enseignants, des VDP agricoles et plusieurs acteurs locaux. Le promoteur a exprimé sa reconnaissance à la PDS de Poa et à Sa Majesté Naaba Kaongo, représentés à la cérémonie, ainsi qu’aux participants, notamment aux jeunes mobilisés pour le creusage des trous et la mise en terre des plants. Le directeur du Centre de formation de Tondo-Tenga d’Ampo, Olivier Bado, a invité les jeunes à faire bon usage du site. Selon lui, l’espace peut contribuer au développement de l’agriculture et de l’élevage. Il a assuré que son centre est disposé à accompagner et à former les jeunes afin de faire du site un véritable centre d’excellence. Olivier Bado a également appelé les jeunes à ne pas abandonner leurs études au profit de l’orpaillage. Il les a encouragés à privilégier la formation, l’agriculture et l’élevage, rappelant qu’aucun métier honnête n’est indigne. Il a par ailleurs indiqué que son centre est prêt à accompagner les coopératives sérieuses. Pour Ambroise Nabi, secrétaire général de la CNVC de Nando, planter un arbre contribue à la préservation de la forêt. Il a souhaité que le site devienne un espace de formation au profit des jeunes dans les domaines de l’agriculture et de l’élevage. Il a également invité les autorités communales à identifier les jeunes réellement intéressés par ces activités afin de mieux les accompagner. Il a félicité le promoteur et salué la présence des VDP agricoles et des enseignants. Représentant la PDS de Poa, le secrétaire général de la commune, Ousmane Sawadogo, a salué cette initiative, qu’il considère comme un éveil des consciences. Il a rappelé que les jeunes constituent la relève de la nation et que la plantation d’arbres doit être accompagnée d’un entretien régulier pour garantir leur survie. Agence d'information du Burkina MK/PB/AS/ATA

items.title: Sanguié/Pouni : Les directeurs d’écoles outillés en bi-plurilinguisme et pour la rentrée 2026-2027
items.description: BURKINA-SANGUIE-POUNI-EDUCATION-RENTREE-PREPARATIFS Sanguié/Pouni : Les directeurs d’écoles outillés en bi-plurilinguisme et pour la rentrée 2026-2027 Tita, 13 sept. 2026 (AIB) – Les directeurs d’écoles de la commune de Pouni ont pris part, le vendredi 11 septembre, à l’école Tita C, à une rencontre de cadrage axée sur la généralisation du bi-plurilinguisme, les mouvements du personnel et les préparatifs de la rentrée scolaire 2026-2027. Présidée par le Chef de la circonscription d’éducation de base (CCEB) de Pouni, Bahini Edmon Coulibaly, cette assise visait à doter les premiers responsables d’établissements des orientations nécessaires pour une année scolaire réussie. La généralisation de l'approche bi-plurilingue a constitué le premier point inscrit à l’ordre du jour. Cette réforme pédagogique vise à optimiser les apprentissages fondamentaux en combinant l'utilisation des langues nationales et du français. Abordant la question des affectations pour nécessité de service, le CCEB a expliqué qu'outre la régulation des effectifs, ces mouvements répondent à un impératif d'équité pour renforcer qualitativement les équipes éducatives dans les zones qui en expriment le besoin. Le chapitre des divers a permis de rappeler des échéances cruciales, parmi lesquelles la tenue obligatoire des conseils d'enseignants fixée au 15 septembre prochain, ainsi que la stricte rigueur exigée dans le signalement des cas d'absence. S'adressant aux participants, le premier responsable de l'éducation de base dans la commune a insisté sur l'exercice d'un leadership managérial affirmé. Il a invité les directeurs à rationaliser l'affectation des enseignants au sein de leurs structures en tenant compte des compétences spécifiques et des profils recherchés pour maximiser le rendement scolaire. Mettant un accent particulier sur les classes d'examen du CM2, le camarade Coulibaly a préconisé une mobilisation collégiale. « Pour nos classes de CM2, je compte sur la mobilisation de toute l’équipe pédagogique autour de l’enseignant titulaire. C’est dans l’union et l’engagement de tous que nous garantirons de meilleurs résultats à nos élèves », a-t-il exhorté. Agence d'information du Burkina JS/PB/AS/ATA

items.title: It’s All Fun and Games Until You Give AI Your Credit Card
items.description: In the race to develop intelligent machines, the leading AI companies have built bots that can whip up spreadsheets at a moment’s notice, write sophisticated code, and even solve long-standing math problems. But when it comes to the more mundane tasks of life—such as ordering groceries or booking flights—these tools sometimes still struggle. Now a new bot called Instinct is outperforming the AI giants. Instinct lets people ask for help with all kinds of tasks by texting the bot directly through iMessage or WhatsApp. Lately, it has been all the rage in the tech world. Online, people are breathlessly sharing examples of what they’ve gotten the tool to do. One person reported that he has turned to Instinct to pay tolls, book a DMV appointment, and even negotiate prices with vendors in India while he sleeps. Another says he used Instinct to ship an Apple Pencil he had left behind at a hotel in Montreal back to him in Brooklyn. Noah Shinn, a 23-year-old Northeastern University dropout, launched the product to a small test group earlier this year, and his company is already worth billions of dollars. As of Thursday, the company is reportedly seeking $1 billion in new funds, which could make it worth the equivalent of Lufthansa or Pinterest. Instinct isn’t the first AI personal assistant to draw attention this year. In the winter, the tech industry fawned over a similar tool called OpenClaw. But Instinct is comparatively much easier to use. Once you create an account, the bot can hook up to your credit cards and all kinds of digital services, including Slack, Google Workspace, and 1Password. Instead of finding a dinner recipe and opening up Instacart to manually add groceries, tell Instinct that you feel like making quiche Lorraine, and it can order groceries for you. But once AI tools start acting on people’s behalf in the real world, mistakes don’t just look like hallucinations. When AI agents have access to your email inbox and credit-card information, all sorts of strange things can go wrong. I downloaded the tool this week to test it out for myself. Using the bot feels a lot like texting an actual person. It uses emojis such as 🫡 and 👀to react to requests as it receives them, and the infamous three dots appear when it’s writing a response. Sometimes, the bot even leaves you on read while it works. (Compare that with ChatGPT, which is always vomiting up walls of text and asking goading follow-up questions.) When I gave my agent a $25 budget and asked it to surprise my editor with a book, the bot read his previous writing (at my instruction), found a book he might enjoy— Material World by Ed Conway—and sent an email alerting him that it was ready for pick-up at his local Barnes & Noble. (Mercifully, Instinct didn’t hack his inbox to see whether he had previously ordered the book; these days, you never know .) The bot also helped me find an Airbnb for an upcoming vacation, track down new in-network primary-care providers, and reach out to cleaning companies to get quotes for a friend. [ Read: Chatbait is taking over the internet ] Other people are outsourcing even more tasks to Instinct. A colleague of mine who has also been testing out the bot used it to book tickets to a museum in Mexico City. The museum was sold out for the dates he wanted, but the bot dutifully monitored the portal for three days and eventually snagged tickets when spots freed up. After the bot paid for the tickets, it rearranged his itinerary—swapping around restaurant reservations—to account for the new schedule. For the time being, Instinct is still available only to a private test group, and perhaps this is for the best. Although the bot is plenty powerful, it’s far from perfect. Online, the mishaps are starting to pile up. One user recently complained on X that Instinct lost him more than $200 after it prematurely canceled his flight. He reported that the bot texted him the following: “Straight story: while pulling up the cancel terms, the cancellation actually went through before I could show you the cost first.” When a man in Los Angeles asked Instinct to scan for restaurant reservations for an upcoming trip, the bot apparently made a reservation without his approval at a place that charged a $200 cancellation fee. Another user temporarily lost access to his Resy account after trying to get a reservation at a hot West Village steak house— without his knowledge , the bot had been spamming the platform with requests. (Shinn, the Instinct founder, did not respond to a request for comment.) Consider, too, the major risks that come with giving an AI agent broad access to your digital life. Ask the bot to respond to a scheduling text from a friend and it could accidentally leak private information: I can’t get lunch on Thursday morning because we have an appointment with our divorce lawyer. But how about dinner ? Hackers could also trick the bot by telling it to ignore previous instructions and forward along any sensitive financial emails. “Despite our reasonable efforts to protect your information, no security measures are impenetrable, and we cannot guarantee ‘perfect security,’” reads Instinct’s privacy policy. While testing Instinct, I used a temporary phone number and did not connect the bot to my email or other important personal accounts; even the credit-card information I gave the bot was for a new, virtual credit-card that I disabled immediately after I was finished experimenting—at which point, I promptly deleted my account. For all of its hazards, Instinct is a harbinger of where AI is headed. Earlier this week, Meta released its own personal-assistant product called Muse. In announcing Muse, Mark Zuckerberg emphasized the company’s security protections; how well those safeguards actually hold up remains to be seen. Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic may well follow suit by refining their own bots to have more Instinct-like capabilities. After all, the tech industry has long dreamed of a moment when a computer can serve as a genuinely competent personal assistant. Even if such bots aren’t quite ready for prime time, early adopters hint at how the technology might shape the world in the years to come. Contrary to the narrative of AI wiping out jobs, these new assistants could end up creating more work—in ways that are not always appealing. In one of the wildest Instinct examples that I encountered, Olivia Levine, an investor in New York, recounted using Instinct to track down footage of her and her boyfriend on the jumbotron at the US Open. As Levine tells it, the couple gave the bot a selfie and their seat numbers. The agent then put out a flurry of requests to the United States Tennis Association, the ticket office, the US Open’s production company, and an American Express media contact. By the following afternoon, a producer had emailed her the footage. A world full of agents seems at once busier and lonelier. On Wednesday, Instinct added a new way for agents to coordinate between themselves. As Shinn explained on X, if you’re planning a weekend trip with friends or making plans with your spouse, you could just have your agents work together to figure out the logistics instead. At least for now, the bots haven’t conquered everything. When I asked it for help finding a new desk chair, Instinct quickly tracked down a great option nearby on Craigslist and drafted a pick-up request to send to the lister. But when it came time to actually send the message, the bot was stymied by a CAPTCHA. I asked the agent to try harder, but it was stuck. “Nothing punctures the fantasy of autonomous intelligence like being defeated by nine blurry crosswalks,” the bot messaged me.

items.title: Ebola : l’Ouganda impose une quarantaine de 21 jours aux élèves en provenance de la RDC
items.description: L’Ouganda a renforcé ses mesures de prévention contre la maladie à virus Ebola dans le secteur de l’éducation. Désormais, les élèves en provenance de la République démocratique du Congo devront observer une quarantaine supervisée de 21 jours avant d’être autorisés à intégrer ou réintégrer leurs établissements scolaires en territoire ougandais.

items.title: FIA allowed to arrest Unity Foods’ CEO in graft case
items.description: KARACHI: The Sindh High Court has suspended an administrative order of a magistrate exonerating the chief executive officer of a private firm in a graft case, and allowed the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) to arrest him for interrogation. The court was informed, however, that the suspect had obtained interim pre-arrest bail until Sept 14. The high court ruled that, following suspension of the magistrate’s order, any subsequent bail order in the matter would have no legal effect. On Aug 30, a judicial magistrate (Karachi East) discharged Muhammad Farrukh Amin Godil, CEO of Unity Foods Limited, a listed company operating in the edible oil and rice sectors, after refusing the FIA’s request for his physical remand for further interrogation and investigation. Other suspects, including Jalees Edhi, Amir Shehzad, Safdar Sajjad and Abdul Majeed Ghaziani, were remanded in FIA custody. The state, through Additional Attorney General Barrister Mohsin Shahwani, subsequently filed a criminal miscellaneous application challenging the magistrate’s order. SHC suspends magistrate’s order exonerating Godil, says subsequent bail order against suspect has no legal effect He argued that the magistrate had misapplied an April order of the SHC restraining authorities from taking coercive action against the suspect. The AAG said that order had no nexus with the present case and had been passed in a separate inquiry under the money-laundering law. He contended that Mr Godil was a primary accused in an FIR concerning alleged corporate crime and that the magistrate should not have discharged him without considering the distinction between the two matters. A single-judge bench headed by Justice Miran Muhammad Shah observed that the magistrate was duty-bound to decide the remand matter urgently without disturbing the status quo of the investigation. The magistrate was required only to accept or reject the remand request and could not pass any other order. “Any such discharge or any other order to that effect passed by the learned duty magistrate was patently illegal and in violation of the law,” the bench observed. While suspending the impugned order until Sept 30, the bench allowed the FIA investigating officer to take the suspect into custody for questioning and investigation. Referring to a Supreme Court judgment, the bench held that once the administrative order had been suspended, the entire structure based on it had fallen and any subsequent bail order would have no legal effect. The court issued notice to the suspect for Sept 30 and directed the AAG to proceed in accordance with its observations. The FIA registered the case against Mr Godil and other company officials on a reference from the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP). According to the FIR, Mr Godil allegedly misappropriated Rs5.318 million of entrusted funds in favour of his mother, Fehmida Amin, under the guise of a “loan”. The SECP referral also cited an internal analysis showing a difference of around Rs44.7 billion between the company’s published accounts and its internal SAP records. Published in Dawn, September 13th, 2026

items.title: Le Kremlin n’exclut pas une reprise des négociations trilatérales entre la Russie, l’Ukraine et les Etats-Unis en octobre
items.description: Le porte-parole du Kremlin Dmitri Peskov a confirmé ce dimanche envisager une telle possibilité. Volodymyr Zelensky, de son côté, avait dit mardi tabler sur une reprise dès septembre des pourparlers, pour tenter de mettre fin à plus de quatre ans et demi de conflit.
